lessons.title: Preparing Jars: Washing, Sterilizing, and Drying
lessons.body: Start by washing jars in hot soapy water. Use a bottle brush to scrub inside, especially if jars held oily foods. Rinse well. You need clean jars with no cracks or chips, and two-piece lids (flat disc and screw band) that are not rusty. For sterilizing, you have three practical options in an African kitchen. First, boiling: place jars and lids in a large pot, cover with water, boil for 10 minutes. Remove with clean tongs and place upside down on a clean cloth to dry. Second, oven: preheat oven to 120Â°C, place washed jars (without lids) on a baking tray, heat for 20 minutes. Lids can be boiled separately for 5 minutes. Third, steam: use a pot with a steamer insert, steam jars for 10 minutes. Whichever method, do not dry with a clothâair dry or use the ovenâs heat. Cloths can recontaminate. Jars must be hot when you fill them with hot jam. If they cool, reheat in oven for 5 minutes. Always fill jars to within 1 cm of the rim. Wipe rim with a clean damp cloth, then place lid and screw band finger-tight. Do not overtighten. After filling, process in a hot water bath (see Lesson 5) for a proper seal. If you skip sterilizing, mold and bacteria will spoil your jam within weeks. In hot African climates, sterilization is not optional. Work quickly and keep everything clean. Use tongs, not fingers. Have a clean towel under jars to catch drips. Prepare jars just before jam is ready, not hours ahead. For a small batch, 6 to 8 jars of 250 ml each is typical. Always make extra sterilized jars in case you have more jam than expected.

lessons.title: Mashing, Chopping, and Preparing Fruit
lessons.body: The texture of your jam depends on how you prepare the fruit. For a smooth jam, mash fruit thoroughly with a potato masher or wooden spoon. For a chunky jam, chop fruit into 1 cm cubes. Some fruits like mango, pawpaw, and pineapple are best chopped. Berries and soft fruits like guava can be mashed. Always remove skins, seeds, and cores unless the recipe says otherwise. For example, mango skin and seed must be removed. Pineapple core is toughâremove it. Citrus fruits need peeling and seeding. Weigh fruit after preparation. A standard ratio is 1 kg prepared fruit to 750 g sugar. If fruit is very sweet, reduce sugar to 600 g. If tart, use up to 1 kg. Add lemon juice: 2 tablespoons per kg of fruit. Lemon juice adds acid, which helps set and preserves color. For low-acid fruits like mango and pawpaw, acid is critical. Let fruit and sugar sit for 1 hour. This draws out juice, so you need less added water. Then mash or chop as desired. If you want seedless jam, put seeds and skins in a muslin cloth and boil with fruit, then remove. For a smoother jam, after cooking, press through a sieve or blend carefully. But blending hot jam is dangerousâcool slightly first. In Africa, fruits vary in water content. Mangoes in dry season are firmer; in rainy season, juicier. Adjust by adding 1-2 tablespoons of lemon juice or a small amount of pectin if available. Never use overripe or rotten fruit. One bad spot can spoil the whole batch. Wash all fruit well. For bananas, use ripe but firm ones; mash with a fork. For tomatoes (yes, tomato jam is common), peel, seed, and chop. Always taste fruit before starting. If it lacks flavor, your jam will too. Add a pinch of salt to enhance sweetness. Prepare fruit in batches no larger than 2 kg to ensure even cooking.

lessons.title: Cooking Methods: Open Kettle vs. Water Bath
lessons.body: There are two main cooking methods for jam: open kettle and water bath. Open kettle means you cook jam in a wide pot on the stove, stirring often, until it reaches set point. This is the traditional method in many African homes. Use a heavy-bottomed pot to prevent burning. Stainless steel or enamel is best; avoid aluminium as it reacts with acid. Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly with a long wooden spoon. Skim off foam with a metal spoon. The jam is ready when it sheets off the spoon (see Lesson 4). This method is fast and gives a rich flavor, but you must watch closelyâjam can burn in seconds. Water bath method means you cook jam first in a pot, then process filled jars in a boiling water bath. The cooking step is the same as open kettle, but after filling jars, you submerge them in boiling water for 10-15 minutes. This creates a vacuum seal and kills any mold spores. Water bath canning is safer for long-term storage, especially in hot humid climates. For both methods, use a thermometer if possible. Jam sets at 104-105Â°C (219-221Â°F) at sea level. At higher altitudes, subtract 1Â°C per 300 m. In Africa, many areas are above 1000 m, so adjust: at 1500 m, set point is about 100-101Â°C. If you donât have a thermometer, use the sheet or drop test. Open kettle jam must be stored in the fridge and eaten within 3 weeks. Water bath processed jam lasts 1 year in a cool dark place. For beginners, start with open kettle for small batches, then move to water bath for larger batches. Always stir from the bottom to prevent scorching. If jam starts to stick, remove from heat immediately and stir vigorously. Never leave jam unattended. Use a timer. A batch of 2 kg fruit takes 20-40 minutes to cook. Test frequently near the end.

lessons.title: Testing for Set: Sheet, Drop, and Thermometer
lessons.body: Knowing when jam is set is the most critical skill. If you undercook, jam is runny. If you overcook, it becomes hard and caramelized. Use three tests. First, the sheet test: dip a cold metal spoon into the jam. Lift it out and let it cool for 5 seconds. Tilt the spoon. If the jam falls in a single sheet or flake rather than dripping, it is set. If it drips like water, cook longer. Second, the drop test: place a small spoonful of jam on a cold plate (put plate in freezer for 5 minutes). Let it cool for 1 minute. Push it with your finger. If it wrinkles and holds its shape, it is set. If it runs, cook longer. Third, thermometer: use a candy or jam thermometer. Clip it to the pot, ensuring the bulb is in the jam but not touching the bottom. Bring jam to 104-105Â°C (219-221Â°F) at sea level. At 1000 m, set point is 103Â°C. At 2000 m, 101Â°C. If you donât have a thermometer, you can calibrate: boil water, note the temperature (e.g., 98Â°C at 1000 m). Then set point is 98 + 4 = 102Â°C. Always test at the end of cooking, not the beginning. Stir jam before testing to ensure even heat. Remove from heat while testing to prevent overcooking. If jam passes the test, skim foam, then fill jars immediately. If it fails, return to heat and boil for 2 more minutes, then test again. Repeat until set. For low-pectin fruits like strawberries, add 1 tablespoon lemon juice per kg to help set. For high-pectin fruits like apples and guavas, set is easier. Never rely on cooking time aloneâfruit moisture varies. A rainy season mango has more water and takes longer. Always use at least two tests. The sheet test is quick; the drop test is more reliable. The thermometer is most accurate. Practice with a small batch of cheap fruit like pawpaw. Over time, you will learn the visual cues: jam thickens, bubbles become slower and larger, and the color deepens.

lessons.title: Hot Water Bath Canning Step-by-Step
lessons.body: Hot water bath canning gives your jam a long shelf life. Follow these steps exactly. 1. Sterilize jars and lids (Lesson 1). Keep jars hot. 2. Fill a large deep pot with water and bring to a rolling boil. The pot must be deep enough to cover jars by 2.5 cm (1 inch). Place a rack or folded cloth at the bottom to prevent jars from touching the pot. 3. Fill hot jars with hot jam, leaving 1 cm headspace. Wipe rims. Place lids and screw bands finger-tight. 4. Use jar tongs to lower jars into boiling water. Do not let jars touch each other. 5. Cover pot and return water to a full boil. Start timing when water boils. Process for 10 minutes for altitudes up to 1000 m. For 1000-3000 m, process 15 minutes. For above 3000 m, 20 minutes. 6. After processing, turn off heat. Wait 5 minutes, then remove jars with tongs. Place on a clean cloth, upright, 5 cm apart. Do not tighten bands. 7. Let cool for 12-24 hours. You may hear a pop as lids seal. After cooling, press the center of each lid. If it does not move, it is sealed. If it pops up and down, it is not sealed. 8. Remove screw bands. Wipe jars. Label with date and fruit. Store in a cool, dark place. Sealed jam lasts 1 year. If any jar did not seal, store in fridge and eat within 3 weeks. Never use a jar with a cracked lid or rust. Never process in a pot that is too small. Always use a timer. For a small batch of 6 jars, use a pot that holds at least 8 liters. In Africa, many homes use a large sufuria or stock pot. That works. Do not use a pressure cooker unless you know the correct settingsâpressure canning is for low-acid foods, not jam. Jam is high-acid, so water bath is safe. If you live at high altitude, increase processing time. Always check seals before storing. If you see mold on the surface after opening, discard the whole jar. Do not scrape it off.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Common Jam Problems
lessons.body: Even experienced cooks face jam problems. Here is how to fix them. Problem 1: Jam is too runny. Cause: undercooked or insufficient pectin. Fix: Return to pot, add 1 tablespoon lemon juice per kg, boil 5-10 minutes, retest. If still runny, add 1 tablespoon powdered pectin (if available) dissolved in a little water. Or cook longer. Problem 2: Jam is too hard. Cause: overcooked or too much sugar. Fix: Once hard, you cannot fully reverse it. Use it as a filling for cakes or melt with a little water for a syrup. Next time, reduce cooking time and test earlier. Problem 3: Jam has mold. Cause: unsterilized jars, dirty lids, or not processed. Fix: Discard the entire jar. Do not eat. Mold produces toxins. Problem 4: Jam has crystals (sugar crystals). Cause: undissolved sugar or too much sugar. Fix: Next time, stir sugar until fully dissolved before boiling. Add 1 teaspoon lemon juice to help prevent. Problem 5: Jam is too sweet. Cause: too much sugar. Fix: Add more lemon juice or a little citric acid. Or mix with tart fruit like tamarind. Problem 6: Jam is too tart. Cause: too little sugar or overripe fruit. Fix: Add a little sugar and reboil. Problem 7: Jam has a burnt taste. Cause: scorching. Fix: Do not stir burnt jam into the rest. Discard burnt batch. Use a heavy-bottomed pot and stir constantly. Problem 8: Jam separates (liquid on top). Cause: insufficient cooking or too much water. Fix: Stir well and reboil for 5 minutes. Problem 9: Lids do not seal. Cause: dirty rim, old lids, or not enough headspace. Fix: Re-process with new lids within 24 hours. Problem 10: Jam ferments (smells like alcohol). Cause: wild yeast from dirty fruit or jars. Fix: Discard. Always wash fruit and sterilize jars. In Africa, high humidity can cause mold faster. Store jam in a cool, dark place. If you are unsure, keep in fridge. Use clean spoons when serving. Never double-dip. A little care prevents most problems.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to dry sterilized jars?
options: A) Wipe with a clean cloth
B) Air dry or use oven heat
C) Dry with a paper towel
quiz.explanation: Cloths or paper towels can recontaminate jars; air drying or oven heat keeps them sterile.

quiz.q: How long should jars be boiled to sterilize them?
quiz.explanation: Boiling for 10 minutes kills most microorganisms on jars and lids.

quiz.q: Why should you not overtighten jar lids before water bath canning?
options: A) It prevents air from escaping during processing
C) It causes jam to burn
quiz.explanation: Air needs to escape during processing to create a proper vacuum seal; overtightening traps air.

quiz.q: What is the recommended headspace when filling jam jars?
quiz.explanation: 1 cm headspace allows for expansion and proper sealing without overflow.

quiz.q: Which fruit preparation gives a chunky jam?
quiz.explanation: Chopping fruit into small cubes preserves pieces, resulting in a chunky texture.

quiz.q: What is the standard ratio of prepared fruit to sugar for jam?
options: A) 1 kg fruit to 500 g sugar
B) 1 kg fruit to 750 g sugar
C) 1 kg fruit to 1 kg sugar
D) 1 kg fruit to 250 g sugar
quiz.explanation: A 1:0.75 ratio is standard; adjust based on fruit sweetness and acidity.

quiz.q: Why is lemon juice added to jam?
options: B) To increase acidity and help set
quiz.explanation: Lemon juice provides acid, which aids pectin setting and enhances preservation and color.

quiz.q: How long should fruit and sugar sit before cooking?
quiz.explanation: Letting them sit for 1 hour draws out juice, reducing the need for added water.

quiz.q: Which pot material is best for cooking jam?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel or enamel are non-reactive; aluminium and copper react with acid and can discolor jam.

quiz.q: What is the open kettle method?
options: A) Cooking jam in a pot and then processing jars
B) Cooking jam in a pot without water bath processing
C) Cooking jam in a water bath
D) Cooking jam in an oven
quiz.explanation: Open kettle means cooking jam and filling jars without a subsequent water bath process.

quiz.q: At what temperature does jam set at sea level?
quiz.explanation: Jam sets at 104-105Â°C at sea level; adjust for altitude.

quiz.q: How do you adjust set temperature at high altitude?
quiz.explanation: Water boils at lower temperatures at altitude, so set point decreases by about 1Â°C per 300 m.

quiz.q: What does the sheet test look for?
options: B) Jam falls in a single sheet from a spoon
quiz.explanation: The sheet test checks if jam falls in a sheet or flake rather than dripping, indicating set.

quiz.q: How do you perform the drop test?
options: A) Drop jam into cold water
B) Place a spoonful on a cold plate and push with finger
C) Drop jam on the floor
D) Drop a thermometer into jam
quiz.explanation: The drop test uses a cold plate; if the cooled jam wrinkles when pushed, it is set.

quiz.q: Why should you remove jam from heat while testing for set?
quiz.explanation: Jam can overcook quickly; removing from heat prevents burning while you test.

quiz.q: What is the correct processing time for water bath canning at altitudes up to 1000 m?
quiz.explanation: 10 minutes is sufficient at low altitudes; increase for higher elevations.

quiz.q: How much water should cover jars in a water bath?
quiz.explanation: Jars should be covered by at least 2.5 cm of boiling water throughout processing.

quiz.q: What should you do after removing jars from water bath?
options: B) Place upright on a cloth to cool
quiz.explanation: Let jars cool upright undisturbed to allow seals to form; do not tighten bands.

quiz.q: How do you know a jar is sealed?
options: B) The center of the lid does not move when pressed
C) The jar makes a sound
quiz.explanation: A sealed lid is concave and does not pop up when pressed.

quiz.q: How long does properly water bath processed jam last?
quiz.explanation: Sealed, processed jam stores well for up to 1 year in a cool, dark place.

quiz.q: What causes sugar crystals in jam?
quiz.explanation: Undissolved sugar can crystallize; stir sugar fully before boiling.

quiz.q: What should you do if jam is too runny?
quiz.explanation: Reboiling with lemon juice adds acid and evaporates water, helping set.

quiz.q: What is the danger of eating jam with mold?
options: C) It is safe if you scrape off mold
quiz.explanation: Mold can produce mycotoxins that are harmful; discard the entire jar.

quiz.q: Why does jam sometimes separate?
quiz.explanation: Separation often means water wasn't fully evaporated; reboil to combine.

quiz.q: What causes fermented jam?
options: A) Wild yeast from dirty fruit or jars
quiz.explanation: Wild yeasts on fruit or in unsterilized jars cause fermentation; always sterilize.

quiz.q: How can you prevent burnt jam?
options: B) Stir constantly and use heavy-bottomed pot
quiz.explanation: Constant stirring and a heavy pot distribute heat evenly, preventing scorching.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store opened jam?
options: A) In a cool, dark place
quiz.explanation: Once opened, jam should be refrigerated to prevent mold growth.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use clean spoons when serving jam?
quiz.explanation: Dirty spoons introduce bacteria and mold, spoiling the jam.

quiz.q: What should you do if a jar fails to seal after water bath?
options: A) Store in fridge and eat within 3 weeks
B) Re-process with new lids within 24 hours
quiz.explanation: You can either refrigerate and use soon, or re-process with new lids if within 24 hours.

quiz.q: Why is lemon juice especially important for mango and pawpaw jam?
quiz.explanation: Mango and pawpaw are low-acid; lemon juice adds acid for set and preservation.
